§0Orientation · LO1

The posterior forearm — the hand's remote control

One compartment, one nerve, one job: open the hand and steady the wrist.

Everything in this lecture hangs off a single idea: the muscles on the back of the forearm are extrinsic muscles of the hand — their bellies sit in the forearm but their long tendons reach across the wrist to work the fingers and thumb. The slide calls them a "remote control": the motor is proximal, the action is distal.

Reasoning · why learn them as one compartment

Three things unify the posterior compartment, so learn it as a block rather than 12 separate muscles. (1) One nerve — every muscle here is supplied by the radial nerve or its deep branch, so a single lesion knocks out the whole group (wrist-drop). (2) One action theme — they extend (elbow, wrist, fingers, thumb) and supinate; they are the antagonists of the anterior flexor compartment you met in L3. (3) One design — bulky bellies proximally taper to long slender tendons that cross the wrist, so force generated in the forearm is delivered precisely to the digits.

Reasoning · why the bellies are proximal and tendons long

Packing muscle mass at the wrist and hand would make them fat and clumsy — you could not thread a needle with sausage fingers. Concentrating the contractile mass in the forearm and running thin tendons distally keeps the hand slim and dexterous while borrowing power from the larger proximal muscles. This is the same 'remote actuator' logic used in robotic hands.

Label Key — Superficial posterior forearm
Brachioradialis
The most lateral muscle; despite living in the extensor compartment it flexes the elbow — the group's odd one out.
Extensor carpi radialis longus
Extends and radially deviates (abducts) the wrist; longus lies proximal to brevis.
Extensor carpi radialis brevis
The main wrist extensor; its origin at the common extensor tendon is the site that fails in tennis elbow.
Extensor digitorum
Occupies most of the posterior surface; its four tendons open the medial four fingers.
Extensor digiti minimi
A slip off extensor digitorum dedicated to the little finger.
Extensor carpi ulnaris
Extends and ulnar-deviates (adducts) the wrist.
Anconeus
Small triangular muscle assisting elbow extension and stabilising the joint.
Extensor retinaculum
A thickening of deep fascia that straps the extensor tendons down at the wrist so they don't bowstring.
R Recall checklist — orientation
  • Compartment — posterior forearm = extensors + supinator; extrinsic (remote) muscles of the hand.
  • Nerve — all supplied by the radial nerve / its deep branch → damage causes wrist-drop.
  • Design — proximal bellies, long distal tendons held down by the extensor retinaculum.
  • Superficial origin — the common extensor tendon on the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
§1Superficial extensors · LO1

The superficial group

Six muscles from the lateral epicondyle — plus one impostor.

The superficial layer is six muscles, five of which share the common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle: brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus & brevis, extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris. Their tendons are strapped at the wrist by the extensor retinaculum (a thickening of the antebrachial fascia).

§1.1Brachioradialis — the exception

As Plate 1.1 shows, brachioradialis lies superficially on the anterolateral forearm. It takes origin high, on the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus, and inserts far down on the lateral surface of the distal radius.

Label Key — Brachioradialis
Lateral supracondylar ridge
Proximal attachment — high on the humerus, giving the muscle a long lever across the elbow.
Brachioradialis belly
Lies anterolaterally; forms the lateral border of the cubital fossa.
Distal radius (lateral surface, near styloid)
Insertion — because it is so far from the elbow axis it is a strong elbow flexor.
Radial nerve
Supplies it directly — one of the few muscles the radial nerve reaches before dividing.
Reasoning · why it flexes when its neighbours extend

Brachioradialis is in the extensor compartment and carried by the radial nerve, so you'd expect it to extend — but it doesn't cross the wrist, and its line of pull runs in front of the elbow's flexion–extension axis. A muscle's action is decided by which side of the joint axis its tendon passes, not by which compartment it lives in. Passing anterior to the elbow axis makes it a flexor of the forearm, strongest in mid-pronation (the 'hitchhiker' or corkscrew-pulling position).

Memory hook · the odd one out

"Radial nerve, but a flexor's job."

Everyone else in the back extends and crosses the wrist. Brachioradialis does neither — it flexes the elbow and stops at the radius. Remember it as the impostor in the extensor room.

§1.2The wrist movers — ECRL, ECRB & ECU

Three muscles run to the metacarpals to drive the wrist itself. Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis extend the wrist; extensor carpi ulnaris extends it too. Their real cleverness is in pairs — see Plate 1.2.

Label Key — Radial & ulnar wrist extensors
Extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL)
Inserts on the 2nd metacarpal base; extends + radially deviates the wrist.
Extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB)
Inserts on the 3rd metacarpal base; the workhorse wrist extensor.
Extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU)
Inserts on the 5th metacarpal base; extends + ulnar-deviates the wrist.
Radial styloid process
Its length physically blocks radial deviation to ~15° — an anatomical end-stop.
Deep branch of radial nerve
Supplies ECRB and ECU (ECRL often direct from the radial nerve).
Reasoning · how extensors and flexors team up to steer the wrist

Pure extension or flexion needs radial and ulnar muscles firing together. But fire an extensor and a flexor on the same side and their extension/flexion cancels while their side-pull adds: ECRL + flexor carpi radialis = abduction (radial deviation); ECU + flexor carpi ulnaris = adduction (ulnar deviation). Movement at the wrist is a vector sum, not one muscle per direction.

Clinical · why radial deviation is so limited

Radial (abduction) is capped at about 15° because the radial styloid juts further distally than the ulnar styloid and jams against the carpus. Ulnar deviation reaches ~30–40°. That asymmetry matters after a Colles' fracture of the distal radius: if the radial styloid heals shortened, the geometry — and grip mechanics — change.

§1.3The finger openers — extensor digitorum & digiti minimi

Extensor digitorum is the principal finger extensor: from the lateral epicondyle it fans into four tendons to the medial four digits, occupying most of the back of the forearm (Plate 1.3). Extensor digiti minimi is a partially detached slip of it, running deep to the retinaculum to reach the 5th digit — extending it chiefly at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint, secondarily at the IP joints.

Label Key — Finger extensors
Extensor digitorum (common)
Four tendons to digits 2–5; the main opener of the fingers.
Extensor digiti minimi
Independent extensor of the little finger (lets you extend it alone).
Extensor tendons on dorsum
Visible converging toward the extensor expansions of the fingers.
Deep branch of radial nerve
Motor supply to both.

§1.4The extensor expansion (dorsal hood)

How does one tendon extend three phalanges? By flattening over the finger into an extensor expansion — a triangular aponeurosis over the dorsum of each medial four digit (Plate 1.4). Each expansion splits into a medial (central) band to the middle phalanx and two lateral bands that reunite on the distal phalanx. Crucially, the lumbricals and dorsal interossei insert into it.

Label Key — Extensor expansion
Extensor digitorum tendon
Delivers extension force onto the dorsum of the finger.
Medial (central) band
Inserts on the base of the middle phalanx — extends the PIP joint.
Two lateral bands
Rejoin to insert on the distal phalanx — extend the DIP joint.
Lumbricals / dorsal interossei
Pull on the expansion — because they pass volar to the MCP and dorsal to the IP joints, they flex MCP and extend the IP joints simultaneously (the 'writing' grip).
Reasoning · why the hood is the key to fine finger control

The extensor expansion is a force-distribution web: it lets a single long extensor open all three finger joints, and it gives the small intrinsic hand muscles (lumbricals, interossei) a dorsal attachment. That is why the intrinsics can flex the knuckle yet straighten the fingertip — the anatomy of neat handwriting and of the 'claw hand' that appears when the intrinsics fail.

Clinical · lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow)

Overuse of the extensor–supinator muscles causes microtrauma at their common tendon on the lateral epicondyle — especially ECRB and ECRL. Risk: repetitive wrist extension — the tennis backhand, but also painters, plumbers, carpenters and musicians (violinists, guitarists). Symptom: pain over the lateral epicondyle that worsens with resisted wrist extension. It is a degenerative tendinopathy, not true inflammation — which is why rest and load management, not just anti-inflammatories, are the mainstay.

Treatment is largely conservative, and stretching the extensor origin (Plate 1.5) offloads the failing tendon.

Label Key — Tennis-elbow stretch
Elbow extended, wrist flexed + pronated
Lengthens the common extensor origin — the passive stretch shown on the slide.
Rest / ice / activity modification
Stop heavy wrist extension for ~6–12 weeks so the tendon can remodel.
NSAIDs
For symptom relief; the core problem is tendon overload, so load management matters most.
R Recall checklist — superficial group
  • Common origin — lateral epicondyle (except brachioradialis, from the supracondylar ridge).
  • Brachioradialis — extensor compartment but a flexor of the elbow; doesn't cross the wrist.
  • ECRL/ECRB + FCR → radial deviation (limited to ~15° by the radial styloid); ECU + FCU → ulnar deviation.
  • Extensor digitorum → 4 tendons to digits 2–5; EDM → independent little-finger extension.
  • Extensor expansion — central band → middle phalanx, lateral bands → distal phalanx; lumbricals/interossei insert.
  • Tennis elbow — ECRB microtrauma at the common extensor origin; pain worse on resisted wrist extension.
§2Deep extensors · LO1

The deep group

The supinator and the outcropping thumb muscles — and the nerve that threads between them.

Five deep muscles: the supinator, and four that emerge ("outcrop") to the thumb and index — abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis. All are driven by the posterior interosseous nerve, the deep branch of the radial nerve after it pierces the supinator.

§2.1Supinator

The supinator forms the floor of the cubital fossa. As Plate 2.1 shows, it spirals anteriorly from a broad origin (lateral epicondyle, radial collateral & annular ligaments, and the supinator crest of the ulna) to wrap the proximal radius. The deep branch of the radial nerve passes between its two heads, dividing it into superficial and deep parts.

Label Key — Supinator
Superficial head (from lateral epicondyle)
Wraps the radius; the deep radial nerve runs deep to it.
Deep head (supinator crest of ulna)
Anchors the muscle so it can rotate the radius, not just pull it.
Proximal radius (insertion)
Winding the muscle around the radius lets it unwind the bone into supination.
Deep branch of radial nerve
Passes between the heads (through the arcade of Frohse) and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.
Clinical · posterior interosseous nerve entrapment

Because the deep radial nerve threads through the supinator (under the arcade of Frohse), a hypertrophied or inflamed supinator can compress it — posterior interosseous nerve syndrome. The result is weak finger/thumb extension (a 'finger drop') but, tellingly, no sensory loss and preserved wrist extension via ECRL — because the nerve is purely motor at that point and ECRL is already supplied more proximally.

Supination has two engines that split the work by elbow position (Plate 2.2).

Label Key — Supination engines
Biceps brachii
The powerful supinator — but only with the elbow flexed (e.g. driving a screw with a screwdriver).
Supinator muscle
The everyday supinator — dominant with the elbow extended, and for slow, unresisted turning.
Elbow position
Determines which muscle has the mechanical advantage — the exam's favourite twist.
Memory hook · flex to fix a screw

"Flexed = biceps, extended = supinator."

A right-handed screw tightens with supination. You instinctively flex the elbow to power it — that recruits biceps, the strong supinator. Elbow flexed → biceps; elbow straight → supinator.

§2.2The thumb outcrop — APL, EPB, EPL & extensor indicis

Three muscles run to the thumb, ordered lateral → medial, plus an independent extensor for the index (Plate 2.3):

  • Abductor pollicis longus (APL) — abducts and extends the thumb at the carpometacarpal (CMC) joint.
  • Extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) — extends the proximal phalanx of the thumb.
  • Extensor pollicis longus (EPL) — extends the distal phalanx at both the MCP and IP joints; it hooks around Lister's tubercle on the dorsal radius as a pulley.
  • Extensor indicis — gives the index finger independent extension (pointing).
Label Key — Thumb & index extensors
Abductor pollicis longus
Most lateral; pulls the thumb metacarpal away from the palm (abduction) and back (extension).
Extensor pollicis brevis
Extends the proximal phalanx; with APL it forms the lateral border of the snuffbox.
Extensor pollicis longus
Extends the thumb tip; uses Lister's tubercle as a pulley and forms the medial snuffbox border.
Extensor indicis
Independent index extension; useful for pointing and testing PIN function.
Posterior interosseous nerve
The continuation of the deep radial nerve — supplies all four.

§2.3The anatomical snuffbox

Abduct and extend the thumb and a triangular hollow appears on the radial wrist — the anatomical snuffbox (Plate 2.4). Its borders and floor are a clinical map:

Label Key — Anatomical snuffbox
Medial border — EPL tendon
One wall of the triangle; the tendon that hooks Lister's tubercle.
Lateral border — EPB + APL tendons
The other wall of the triangle.
Floor — scaphoid & trapezium
The carpal bones you press on when palpating the box — key to scaphoid injury.
Radial artery
Crosses the floor — its pulse is palpable here.
Superficial radial nerve & cephalic vein tributaries
Run in the superficial fascia over the box.
Clinical · why snuffbox tenderness means a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise

The scaphoid forms the snuffbox floor, so a fall on the outstretched hand that fractures it produces exact tenderness in the snuffbox. The scaphoid's blood supply enters distally and runs retrograde, so a fracture across its waist can cut off the proximal fragment → avascular necrosis and non-union. A scaphoid fracture is also easily missed on the first X-ray — hence the rule: snuffbox tenderness = immobilise and re-image, don't dismiss.

§2.4Extensor retinaculum & synovial sheaths

Where all these tendons cross the back of the wrist they are strapped down by the extensor retinaculum and wrapped in synovial sheaths (Plate 2.5) that reduce friction between tendon and bone. The retinaculum divides the space into six compartments, each a named tendon group.

Label Key — Dorsal synovial sheaths
Extensor retinaculum
Holds the tendons against the wrist so they don't 'bowstring' on extension.
Synovial tendon sheaths
Fluid-filled sleeves that lubricate the tendons where they angle over bone.
Six osteofibrous compartments
Each carries a defined tendon set — the anatomical basis of De Quervain's (compartment 1) tenosynovitis.
Reasoning · why tendons need retinacula and sheaths

A tendon that turns a corner over a moving joint would bowstring away from the bone on contraction (wasting excursion) and chafe against the bone. The retinaculum is a pulley that keeps the tendon on its efficient path; the synovial sheath is the bearing that lets it glide with almost no friction. Lose either and you get pain, snapping and wear — e.g. De Quervain's tenosynovitis of the APL/EPB sheath.

R Recall checklist — deep group
  • Supinator — floor of the cubital fossa; deep radial nerve pierces it → becomes the posterior interosseous nerve.
  • Biceps supinates with the elbow flexed; supinator with the elbow extended.
  • Thumb outcrop (lateral→medial) — APL, EPB, EPL (+ extensor indicis); all via the PIN.
  • Snuffbox — borders EPL (medial) vs EPB+APL (lateral); floor scaphoid + trapezium; radial artery within.
  • Snuffbox tenderness = scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise (risk of avascular necrosis).
  • Extensor retinaculum → 6 compartments; synovial sheaths cut tendon friction.
§3Bones of the hand · LO2

Bones of the hand

Eight carpals, five metacarpals, fourteen phalanges — the scaffold the tendons move.

The hand skeleton is three tiers: 8 carpals in two rows, 5 metacarpals, and 14 phalanges (two in the thumb, three in each finger). You need the carpals by name and position because they build the wrist joint and the snuffbox floor.

Label Key — Hand — palmar view
Proximal carpal row (lateral→medial)
Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform — the row that articulates with the radius.
Distal carpal row (lateral→medial)
Trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate — the row that meets the metacarpals.
Metacarpals I–V
Numbered from the thumb; each has a base, shaft and head (the knuckle).
Phalanges
Thumb = proximal + distal; fingers = proximal + middle + distal.
Label Key — Hand — posterior view
Carpals (dorsal aspect)
Same eight bones seen from behind — the surface you palpate through the snuffbox.
Metacarpal heads
Form the knuckles; their rounded shape allows finger abduction only when the joint is extended.
Pisiform
A sesamoid in the FCU tendon — sits on the palmar side, so it is hidden in this dorsal view.
Memory hook · naming the eight carpals

"Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle."

Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle — proximal row lateral→medial (Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform) then distal row lateral→medial (Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate).

Each long bone of the hand has the same three parts (Plate 3.3): a proximal base, a shaft, and a distal head.

Label Key — Long-bone parts (metacarpal)
Base
Proximal end — articulates with a carpal (the CMC joint).
Shaft (body)
The tubular middle — where a 'boxer's fracture' of the 5th metacarpal typically breaks.
Head
Distal end — forms the knuckle (MCP joint) with the proximal phalanx.
Label Key — Normal wrist imaging
Plain radiograph
Shows bone outline and joint spaces — first-line for suspected fracture (though scaphoid # can hide).
Coronal MRI
Shows the carpal bones, articular cartilage and the articular disc — used when X-ray is normal but injury is suspected.
Even carpal alignment
The smooth arcs of the carpal rows (Gilula's lines) — a break in the arc signals dislocation.
Clinical · why the carpals are a common blind spot

Carpal injuries are frequently missed because the eight small bones overlap on a flat X-ray. The scaphoid (fracture) and the lunate (dislocation) cause the most trouble — both can lead to chronic wrist pain and arthritis if missed. Knowing the normal arrangement (Plates 3.1–3.2) and imaging (Plate 3.4) is what lets you spot the abnormal.

R Recall checklist — bones of the hand
  • 8 carpals — proximal: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; distal: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.
  • Scaphoid — floor of the snuffbox; most commonly fractured carpal (AVN risk).
  • 5 metacarpals + 14 phalanges — thumb has 2 phalanges, each finger 3.
  • Each long bone = base (proximal) · shaft · head (distal).
§4Wrist joint · LO3

The wrist (radiocarpal) joint

A synovial condyloid joint — radius and disc on top, scaphoid and lunate below.

The true wrist joint is the radiocarpal joint: a synovial condyloid (ellipsoid) joint. The distal radius and an articular disc form the socket; the scaphoid and lunate (and, in ulnar deviation, the triquetrum) form the ball. Note what's absent: the ulna does not reach the carpus — the articular disc separates it from the bones (Plate 4.1).

Label Key — Wrist articular surfaces
Distal radius facets
Two facets take the scaphoid (lateral) and lunate (medial) — the radius bears the load of the hand.
Articular (triangular fibrocartilage) disc
Caps the ulnar head and separates the ulna from the carpals — a shock-absorbing spacer.
Ulnar head
Excluded from the wrist joint proper — it articulates with the radius (distal radioulnar joint), not the carpus.
Ulnar notch of radius
Where the radius meets the ulna — the pivot for pronation/supination.
Reasoning · why the radius, not the ulna, carries the hand

The hand hangs off the radius: the radius widens distally into a facet-bearing surface for the carpals, while the ulna is held off by the disc. That is the whole logic of pronation/supination — the radius (with the hand) rotates around the fixed ulna. It also explains why a fall on the outstretched hand transmits force straight up the radius and fractures its distal end (Colles' fracture), not the ulna.

§4.1Capsule & ligaments

A fibrous capsule surrounds the joint, reinforced on every side (Plate 4.2): the palmar and dorsal radiocarpal ligaments front and back, the ulnar collateral ligament medially and the radial collateral ligament laterally.

Label Key — Wrist ligaments
Palmar radiocarpal ligament
Strong anterior strap; angled so the hand follows the forearm into supination and stays stable.
Dorsal radiocarpal ligament
Posterior strap; tightens in flexion.
Radial collateral ligament
Lateral — limits ulnar deviation (checks the wrist tipping medially).
Ulnar collateral ligament
Medial — limits radial deviation.
Fibrous capsule
Encloses the synovial joint and anchors the ligaments.
Reasoning · why the palmar ligaments are the strongest

The palmar radiocarpal ligaments are thicker than the dorsal ones because we habitually take load on an extended wrist (pushing up, breaking a fall), which tensions the palmar side. The ligaments are also oriented to guide the carpus so the hand tracks the forearm during supination. When they fail, the carpus can slide — carpal instability.

§4.2Movements

The condyloid shape allows movement in two planes, and their combination (Plate 4.3):

Movements of the wrist and their prime movers
MovementPrime moversAssisted by
ExtensionECRL, ECRB, ECUExtensors of the digits
FlexionFCR, FCUFlexors of the digits, palmaris longus
Abduction (radial)ECRL + FCRAPL, EPB (~15°, limited by radial styloid)
Adduction (ulnar)ECU + FCU—
CircumductionSuccessive flexion → adduction → extension → abduction
Label Key — Wrist movements
Flexion / extension
In the sagittal plane — driven by the carpi flexors vs extensors.
Abduction (radial deviation)
Toward the thumb — limited to ~15°.
Adduction (ulnar deviation)
Toward the little finger — the freer of the two side movements.
Circumduction
The four movements run in sequence to sweep the hand in a cone.
Memory hook · deviation = the bone it heads toward

Radial deviation = abduction = hand tips toward the radius/thumb side. Ulnar deviation = adduction = toward the ulna/little-finger side. Name the bone, name the movement.

R Recall checklist — wrist joint
  • Type — synovial condyloid (ellipsoid) radiocarpal joint.
  • Articulation — distal radius + articular disc above; scaphoid + lunate (+ triquetrum) below; ulna excluded.
  • Ligaments — palmar & dorsal radiocarpal (front/back), ulnar & radial collateral (sides).
  • Movements — flexion/extension, radial/ulnar deviation, circumduction; radial deviation capped at ~15°.
§5Bone fractures · LO4

Bone fractures — types & mechanisms

How strong bone still breaks, and how we name the break.

Despite its mineral strength, bone breaks under extreme load, sudden impact, or stress from an unusual direction. Fractures are named by their appearance, location and the nature of the break — and the terms overlap, so a single fracture often carries several descriptors.

The first, most important split is by skin integrity:

  • Closed (simple) fracture — the skin is intact.
  • Compound (open) fracture — the bone breaks the skin. More serious because the wound risks infection and uncontrolled bleeding.
Reasoning · why open fractures are an emergency

An intact envelope of skin keeps the fracture haematoma sterile and contained. Break the skin and you convert a healing problem into a contamination problem: bacteria reach bone (osteomyelitis), and the tamponade that limited bleeding is lost. That is why open fractures need urgent washout and antibiotics, not just reduction.

Label Key — Fracture patterns
Transverse
A straight break across the shaft — from a direct blow (bending force).
Oblique
An angled break — from a force applied along the bone at an angle.
Spiral
A corkscrew break — from a twisting (torsional) force; classic in sports.
Comminuted
Bone shattered into ≥3 fragments — high-energy impact.
Greenstick
An incomplete break bending one cortex — in children's soft, springy bone.
Impacted
Fragments driven into each other — from an axial load (e.g. a fall).

Beyond the pattern, three special mechanisms are worth naming (Plate 5.2):

  • Compression fracture — the bone is crushed, widening or flattening; the classic site is a vertebral body.
  • Pathological fracture — a break through bone already weakened by disease: osteoporosis, osteomalacia, or metastatic tumour (commonly from breast, prostate, thyroid, kidney).
  • Stress fracture — a crack from repetitive loading, typical in the foot bones of athletes, dancers and marching soldiers.
Label Key — Compression & pathological
Fracture line through abnormal bone
Breaks at a site of pre-existing disease (lucency, lesion) rather than the point of maximal force.
Osteoporotic / osteomalacic bone
Reduced mineral or matrix lowers the load the bone can take — 'fragility' fractures.
Metastatic deposit
Secondary tumour (breast, prostate, thyroid, kidney) erodes bone until it fails under normal load.
Clinical · a fracture with no real trauma is a red flag

If a bone breaks after a trivial force, ask why. A pathological fracture can be the first sign of osteoporosis or an occult cancer — a low-energy hip or vertebral fracture in an older adult, or any fracture through a lytic lesion, warrants a look for the underlying disease, not just fixation.

Memory hook · cancers that go to bone

"Lead Kettle" — B, L, T, K, P: Breast, Lung, Thyroid, Kidney, Prostate are the tumours that most love bone. The slide names breast, prostate, thyroid and kidney — add lung and you have the classic five.

Preventing stress fractures (slide 30) is about giving bone time to adapt: increase load slowly, wear comfortable shoes, eat for bone (calcium + vitamin D), cross-train to balance high- and low-impact activity, and avoid sudden changes of training surface (grass → hard court).

Reasoning · why stress fractures are a remodelling failure

Bone constantly remodels to the loads placed on it (Wolff's law — see Bone Physiology I). A stress fracture appears when microdamage accumulates faster than osteoblasts can repair it — too much load, too fast. The prevention advice is really one instruction: don't outrun your bone's rebuilding rate.

R Recall checklist — fractures
  • Closed vs open — open (compound) fractures risk infection + bleeding → emergency.
  • Named by appearance, location and nature; patterns: transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, greenstick, impacted.
  • Compression — crushed bone, classic in the vertebral body.
  • Pathological — through diseased bone (osteoporosis, osteomalacia, mets: breast/prostate/thyroid/kidney).
  • Stress — repetitive overload; prevent by loading slowly + calcium/vit D + cross-training.
§6Bone healing · LO5

How bones heal

The repair cascade that turns a clot into new bone.

Learning outcome 5 asks you to explain how bones heal. Bone is one of the few tissues that repairs with original tissue rather than a scar — a fractured bone can end up as strong as before. Secondary (callus) healing runs in four overlapping stages, each building on the tools you met in Bone Physiology I.

Reasoning · why we cover healing right after fractures

Knowing how a bone breaks is only half the story — the clinical question is always will it heal, and how do I help it? The four-stage cascade below is the direct sequel to the cell biology of bone: the same osteoblasts, osteoclasts and remodelling that build and maintain bone are the ones that rebuild it after a fracture.

  1. Haematoma formation (hours–days) — torn vessels in the bone and periosteum bleed; the clot (fracture haematoma) walls off the site and recruits inflammatory cells. Bone ends deprived of blood die back slightly.
  2. Fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus (days–weeks) — fibroblasts and chondroblasts lay down collagen and cartilage bridging the gap; new capillaries invade. This soft callus splints the fracture but is not yet rigid.
  3. Bony (hard) callus (weeks) — osteoblasts convert the soft callus to woven bone, forming a bulky bony bridge across the fragments. The fracture is now united but over-built and irregular.
  4. Remodelling (months–years) — osteoclasts and osteoblasts reshape the woven bone into compact and spongy bone along the lines of stress (Wolff's law), restoring the original contour and strength.
Clinical · what slows or stops healing

Healing needs blood supply, stability and time. It is impaired by excess movement at the site (why we immobilise), poor blood supply (e.g. the scaphoid waist — §2.3), infection (open fractures), smoking and poor nutrition, advanced age and diseases like diabetes, and some drugs (chronic corticosteroids; NSAIDs are debated). Failure to unite is a non-union; healing in the wrong position is a malunion.

Memory hook · the four-callus story

"Clot, Cartilage, Callus, Contour."

Clot → Cartilage → Compact-ish (woven) → Contoured. Haematoma, soft (cartilage) callus, hard (bony) callus, remodelling — four C's from blood clot to finished bone.

R Recall checklist — bone healing
  • Four stages — haematoma → fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus → bony (hard) callus → remodelling.
  • Repairs with bone, not scar — remodelling restores original strength along stress lines (Wolff's law).
  • Needs blood supply, stability, time; impaired by movement, poor blood supply, infection, smoking, age.
  • Failures — non-union (won't join) and malunion (joins crooked).
